text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish state-owned railway company SJ has for several years secretly paid a political campaign against company cars used by employees. But, helped by lobbying, car manufacturers won a fight and parliament has raised taxes for 1.3 million Swedes in order to finance lower taxes on company cars.

- Carl Bildt is likely to give short notice when he leaves his current position as a peace mediator in Bosnia to return to Sweden to lead the conservative party, the Moderates, Bildt's Swedish staff says. Bildt is likely to return to Sweden late this spring.
- Up to 1,400 jobs could disappear at telecoms group Ericsson's Norrkoping plant in Sweden when the company restructures and outsources its printed board operations.
- Mentally ill people could be just as large a threat to the central government and national security as organised assailants and terrorists, Sweden's secret service said in a report.
- Telecoms group Ericsson has poor profitability on printed boards for its AXE switches and will therefore outsource the operations.
- Unions in blue collar labour union umbrella LO agreed on guidelines for a new wage setting process. Only the transport workers union Transport made a reservation against the decision.

- Investment company Latour, controlled by the family of board chairman Gustaf Douglas, is by far the most succesful Swedish firm when it comes to corporate spin-offs, according to a newspaper analysis.

- Two companies in the Wallenberg family business sphere, traditionally viewed as a rival to the Volvo group, are turning to Volvo to find qualified board members. Volvo chief executive Soren Gyll has accepted an appointment to serve on the board of rolling bearing manufacturer SKF and Volvo vice president Lennart Jeansson has been recommended to serve on the board of engineer Atlas Copco.
- Border trade between Sweden and Norway increased by 40 percent on the Swedish side in January and February, compared to the first two months of 1996.
